questions.prompt: What does Python print?
questions.hint: Look at which name has quote marks around it.
questions.ok: name without quotes is the stored text; "name" in quotes is the word itself. Python prints text without its quote marks.

questions.prompt: Store the supply voltage as a number
questions.hint: Think about what * would do to each option.
questions.ok: 12 is a number, so volts * 2 is 24. In quotes, "12" is text, and text times 2 repeats it: 1212.

questions.prompt: What does the label line print?
questions.hint: Look at where the spaces sit.
questions.ok: str(volts) turns 12 into "12", and + joins the pieces with their spaces: Circuit A at 12 V.

questions.prompt: The technician's script stops. Which line?
questions.hint: Look for a line that mixes two different types.
questions.ok: volts is a number, and + cannot join text to a number, so Python stops. str(volts) fixes it.

questions.prompt: Write the panel label in one line
questions.hint: One letter in front of the quotes changes what the braces do.
questions.ok: An f-string fills each {name} with its value, so no str() is needed: Circuit A: 12 V.

questions.prompt: What current does Python print?
questions.hint: Think about whether Python keeps decimals when it divides.
questions.ok: I = V / R = 12 / 4. Python's / always gives a decimal number, a float, so it prints 3.0. // would give 3.

questions.prompt: Work out the power
questions.hint: Which operation turns volts and amps into watts?
questions.ok: P = V × I = 12 × 3.0 = 36.0 W. ** would raise 12 to a power instead.

questions.prompt: Add 3 Ω in series. What is the current now?
questions.hint: Combine the two resistors first.
questions.ok: 4 Ω + 3 Ω in series is 7 Ω, so I = 12 / 7 = 1.714..., and round(I, 2) gives 1.71.

questions.prompt: Partner's script says 39 W. Which line?
questions.hint: Look at which numbers each operation applies to.
questions.ok: Python works out V ** 2 / 4 first, then adds 3: 36 + 3 = 39.0. It should divide by R_total.

questions.prompt: Is the power under the 25 W rating?
questions.hint: Compare the power with the rating.
questions.ok: P is 144 / 7, about 20.6 W, so P < 25 is True: the resistor stays within its rating.

questions.prompt: How many hours does the battery last?
questions.hint: Think about what / gives in Python.
questions.ok: 2000 / 300 is 6.666... hours. Python prints a float with all its digits.

questions.prompt: How many whole hours?
questions.hint: You want to drop the part after the decimal point.
questions.ok: // is floor division: 2000 // 300 is 6 whole hours.

questions.prompt: What does the runtime line print?
questions.hint: Work out the remainder first, then left to right.
questions.ok: 2000 % 300 is 200 mAh left over; 200 × 60 // 300 is 40 minutes, so it prints 6 h 40 min.

questions.prompt: The club member's script stops. Which line?
questions.hint: Think about what input() gives back.
questions.ok: input() always returns text, so 2000 / "300" fails. Wrap it: int(input("mA: ")).

questions.prompt: Round the runtime to 1 decimal for the poster
questions.hint: round() takes the number and the number of decimals.
questions.ok: round(hours, 1) keeps one decimal: 6.666... becomes 6.7.

questions.prompt: What total power does Python print?
questions.hint: Add the three parts.
questions.ok: 0.5 + 6.0 + 0.25 = 6.75 watts in total.

questions.prompt: What current does a 12 V supply give?
questions.hint: Power is volts times amps.

questions.prompt: Two sensors draw 0.1 W and 0.2 W. What prints?
questions.hint: Some decimals cannot be stored exactly in binary.
questions.ok: 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary form, so the sum is a tiny bit off: 0.30000000000000004. Round before you compare or display.

questions.prompt: Headroom shows 9.325, not 0.325. Which line?
questions.hint: Look at which numbers the division applies to.
questions.ok: Python divides first: 10 - 0.675 = 9.325. Brackets make it (supply - need) / supply = 0.325.

questions.prompt: Is there at least 20% headroom?
questions.hint: 20% as a fraction of 1.
questions.ok: 0.325 >= 0.2 is True: the supply keeps 32.5% headroom.

questions.prompt: The sensor reads 45%. What happens?
questions.hint: Compare the reading with the limit in the code.
questions.ok: 45 > 30 is True, so the pusher bins the spotted orange. The clean apple has no instruction yet, so it rolls off the end.

questions.prompt: Good fruit should stay on the belt
questions.hint: What should the line do when the check fails?
questions.ok: else runs whenever the if check is False: 12 > 30 is False, so the pear stays on the belt. Now every fruit has a place to go.

questions.prompt: The sensor reads 20%. Where does it go?
questions.hint: Python reads the checks from the top.
questions.ok: 20 > 30 is False, then 20 > 15 is True, so the peach goes to the juice line and Python skips the rest.

questions.prompt: The pusher bins good fruit. Which line?
questions.hint: Read the condition aloud and compare it with the rule.
questions.ok: < 30 is True for clean fruit, so the pusher fired on good fruit. Spoilt means more than 30: spots > 30.

questions.prompt: Bin fruit that is spotted or soft
questions.hint: Re-read the question: does the fruit need both problems?
questions.ok: or needs only one condition to be True: 12 > 30 is False, but firm < 2 is True, so the soft pear goes to the bin. and would need both.
